reasons.abstract_intro: Paper A's abstract (p.1) is overlong and crammed with numbers, but its introduction and related work are thorough and well organised; Paper B's abstract is more concise, but its related work is thin and explicitly 'intentionally limited' (p.2).

reasons.title: Paper A's title (p1) is a punchy question with a clear subtitle, while Paper B's (p1) is a similar question but wordier and more awkward.
reasons.figure1: Neither paper has an overview diagram; Paper A's Figure 1 (p5) is a clean two-row results plot with paired-gain panels, more informative than Paper B's six-panel RMSE curves (p4).
reasons.figures_tables: Paper A's tables and figures (pp4-8) are consistent and clean, with bold best entries and CIs; Paper B's Table 2 (p5) and Table 3 (p6) are dense, small-font blocks, and Figure 2's multi-line plots are cluttered.
reasons.experiments: Paper A covers seven matrices, six predictors, many selectors, distribution-shift splits, data-condition ablations (Fig. 2), synthetic theory checks (Fig. 3) and a protocol-pitfall analysis (Table 6); Paper B is solid (family split, data sweeps, theory vs. data) but somewhat narrower.
reasons.page_use: Paper A's body fills about 9 pages (discussion ends p9) with around 22 references; Paper B's body ends on p8 with only about 14 references.
reasons.clean_text: Paper B's body names files (data.md, data_prep.py on p3) and its appendix names results/*.json and .csv files (p10); Paper A keeps the main text clean, with only the pipeline script named in its reproducibility appendix (p12).
reasons.abstract_intro: Paper B's abstract (p1) runs about 30 lines, though its explicit hypotheses H1-H4 are nice; Paper A's abstract is tighter, and its introduction gives clear contributions and a 'findings in brief' (pp1-2).

reasons.title: Both titles ask the same question and are fairly long; B's 'How Many Benchmarks Must You Run? Choosing a Few and Inferring the Rest' (p.1) reads slightly crisper than A's three-line title (p.1).
reasons.figure1: Neither has a mechanism diagram. A's Figure 1 (p.4) is a dense six-panel grid of thin overlapping curves. B's Figure 1 (p.5) pairs R² with paired gain over random and has clearer CI bands, so it is more readable.
reasons.figures_tables: B's figures and tables (pp.5–8) are consistent and clean, including a forest-style data-conditions plot (Fig. 2, p.7). A's tables (Tables 2–3, pp.5–6) use tiny bracketed-CI fonts, and several main tables were pushed to the appendix.
reasons.experiments: Both use six or seven public matrices with bootstrap CIs. B adds new-organisation and temporal shift splits (Table 4, p.7), a broad sweep over history size, missingness, pool and transform (Fig. 2), six predictors and seven selectors, and a protocol-pitfall check (§4.6). B's four propositions are each verified (Fig. 3, p.8), which supports its claims more completely.
reasons.page_use: B's body runs a full 9 pages with about 22 references (pp.1–9). A's body ends on p.8 with only about 13 references.
reasons.clean_text: A's body names a script, 'data_prep.py', and a commit hash (p.3), and its appendix cites results/*.json paths (p.10). B keeps commits in the references and appendix, with only run_everything.sh in Appendix B.2.
reasons.abstract_intro: A's abstract (p.1) is very long and number-heavy, and its introduction is brief, with hypotheses H1–H4. B's abstract is also dense, but B's introduction and related work (pp.1–2) are better argued, with clear contributions and a three-part related-work section.

reasons.title: Paper A's title (page 1) is a direct question that names the problem, though somewhat long; Paper B's title is longer and hedged ('A Descriptive Study of Coverage, Selection, and Dependence').
reasons.figure1: Paper A's Figure 1 (page 5) is a clear multi-panel result plot of R² versus k with gain over random, while Paper B's Figure 1 (page 7) is a plainer budget-curve plot with a source file path in its caption; neither paper has an overview diagram.
reasons.figures_tables: Paper A's tables and figures (pages 4–8) are clean and consistent in style; Paper B's captions repeatedly cite artifact paths such as 'artifacts/summary.csv' (pages 3, 6, 7, 8), and Table 4 (page 14) has awkwardly wrapped intervals.
reasons.experiments: Paper A tests seven matrices with random, organisation and temporal splits, data-condition ablations, a predictor comparison and synthetic checks of its theory (pages 4–8); Paper B rests on 8 candidates and 4 audit tasks, admits a failed feasibility gate, and labels all its results descriptive (pages 1–7).

reasons.abstract_intro: Paper A's abstract and introduction (pages 1–2) state clear questions, contributions and findings in a NeurIPS style; Paper B's abstract (page 1) is defensive, focused on its own failures and disclaimers, and opens with a 'Research draft; not submitted' note.

reasons.title: Paper B's title (p1) is a direct, question-style title that states the task, while Paper A's title (p1) is a long four-line title with a hedging subtitle ('A Descriptive Study of Coverage, Selection, and Dependence').

reasons.title: Paper A's title (page 1) is a catchy question plus a subtitle and is somewhat long. Paper B's title (page 1) is longer and more cumbersome, with three clauses and a 'Budget of k Benchmarks' tail.

Paper B's abstract (page 1) is an overly long block of numbers that is hard to parse, and its prose leans on pipeline language such as 'All numbers come from the shipped code'.

reasons.page_use: Paper B's body fills about nine pages (pages 1–9) before the references and NeurIPS checklist; Paper A's body also reaches about page 9–10, but much of its added length is appendix tables.
